nameStory: The 'yellow' in yellow horned poppy comes from its bright golden-yellow flowers that stand out against coastal landscapes. The 'horned' part refers to its most distinctive feature - long, curved seed pods that can grow up to a foot long and look remarkably like slender horns or sickles jutting out from the plant.
description: Yellow horned poppy is a striking coastal plant that produces large, papery yellow flowers throughout the summer. This short-lived perennial or biennial grows in low, sprawling clumps about 1-3 feet tall and wide. Its most memorable feature is the dramatically long, curved seed pods that give the plant its horn-like appearance. The entire plant has a blue-green, waxy look that helps it survive harsh seaside conditions.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Extremely long, curved seed pods up to 12 inches long that arch outward like horns or sickles - this is the plant's signature feature that nothing else has

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, bright yellow flowers with four papery petals that feel delicate and crinkled like tissue paper, blooming from June through September

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, blue-green leaves with a waxy coating that feels smooth and somewhat rubbery to the touch, deeply lobed with rounded segments

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, sprawling plant that hugs the ground in coastal areas, never found more than a short distance from the ocean

habitat: Yellow horned poppy is strictly a seashore plant, found only along sandy beaches, rocky coastlines, and coastal dunes throughout New England's shoreline. It thrives in the harsh conditions right near the ocean where salt spray, sandy soil, and strong winds would kill most other plants. You'll never find this species inland - it's completely dependent on the coastal environment.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with their distinctive blue-green waxy coating, and the plant begins forming its low, spreading rosette.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flowers bloom continuously from June through September, followed by the development of the characteristic long, curved horn-like seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open to release seeds, while flowers may continue blooming into early fall in protected locations.
seasonality.winter: In mild winters, the waxy blue-green leaves may persist, but the plant often dies back to the ground, surviving as seeds or roots.

funFact: This plant is like a botanical extremist - it's so adapted to coastal life that it literally cannot survive away from the ocean, making it one of the few plants that is 100% dependent on seaside conditions and will never be found even a mile inland.
confusionNotes: The long, curved seed pods make this plant unmistakable - no other New England plant produces anything remotely similar to these dramatic horn-like fruits that can be nearly a foot long.
contextualKnowledge: All parts of yellow horned poppy are toxic and should never be eaten, despite its attractive flowers. It's considered a noxious weed in some parts of North America where it's been introduced, though it remains relatively uncommon in New England coastal areas.
compareHints: Yellow horned poppy is easily distinguished from its relative red horned poppy by its bright yellow flowers versus red or orange ones. Both species share the characteristic long, curved seed pods, but red horned poppy is much rarer in New England and typically has more finely divided leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red Horned Poppy differs from its relative Yellow Horned Poppy by its red flowers with black spots (versus plain yellow flowers) and its smaller, more delicate stature.
